## 1. Game kits
All kits hang off the `game` namespace in `packages/engine/src/agent-api/nodes/game/index.ts`. They are headless, deterministic state machines. They produce state, events and snapshots, not rendering. The scene, art and camera are wired separately (`game.platformerSceneBinding`, `game.racingRoadMesh` and similar).

| Kit | File (absolute, under ``) | Lines | What you get |
|---|---|---|---|
| `game.platformer(level)` | `packages/engine/src/agent-api/GameGenreKits.ts` (`createGamePlatformerKit`, line 997) | The file is 2807 lines in total, shared with racing and falling blocks. | A 2D-plane platformer sim with rect platforms, moving platforms, collectibles, hazards, checkpoints and a finish. It has a surface query, a jump-assist helper and a `GamePlatformerSnapshot`. Level and asset binding helpers (`assetBoundPlatformerLevel`, `platformerCameraRig`) and a geometry certifier sit alongside it. |
| `game.racing(opts)` | same file (`createGameRacingKit`, line 1528) | ~400 lines for the kit; the file is shared | Route or spline-based racing with checkpoints, laps, speed model, AI, and track-topology and surface queries. Also has road mesh, camera rig and start/finish prefabs. |
| `game.fallingBlocks(opts)` | same file (`createGameFallingBlocksKit`, line 1925) | ~880 lines to end of file | Tetromino state machine (`GAME_FALLING_BLOCK_PIECES` I/J/L/O/S/T/Z), with seed, board size and hidden rows. It is a full ruleset with no rendering. |
| `game.fighting(...)` | `packages/engine/src/agent-api/game-kits/fighting.ts` | 671 | 2D-rules fighter kit: stage, controls map, combat moves, hit/hurt/guard/push boxes, combat world, combo/round/health HUD bindings. |

Shared runtime: `packages/engine/src/agent-api/GameRuntime.ts` is 4513 lines. The shell package `packages/game/` (`@aura3d/game`, about 7,000 lines) provides `createGame`, a screen shell (Title, Settings, Results, ContextLost), `GameSession` and lifecycle, a HUD kit with widgets, themes, touch controls (280 lines), juice (tween, fx, rumble, screen overlay), SFX (528 lines) and an art-acceptance audit.

## 2. Templates
Templates live in `templates/`. Each has `index.html`, `package.json`, `aura.assets.json`, `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `playwright.config.ts`, `public/aura-assets` and `tests/`. Line counts below are for `src/`.
- `mini-game/`: 353-line `main.ts` plus 151 lines of typed assets. It is a platformer starter on `game.platformer` and `createGame`, with keyboard input, reset, scoring and a DOM HUD. Its README says it is a "playable starter, not a production game claim".
- `racing-starter/`: 357 lines. A `game.racing` starter.
- `falling-blocks-starter/`: 579 lines. A `game.fallingBlocks` starter.
- `fighting-game/`: 1161 lines across `main.ts` (525), `game/{stage,fighters,moves}.ts` and `styles.css`.
- `character-controller/`: 325 lines across `main.ts` (246), `controller.ts` (44) and assets.
- Extras you didn't list:
  - `arena-shooter/` (672 lines): a top-down 60° shooter. WASD moves, Space fires pooled bolts, a wave spawner lands drones, contact costs shield, R resets.
  - `game-slice/` (236 lines).
  - `templates/` holds about 20 other templates, mostly viewers and configurators.

Shipped showcase games are in `apps/showcase-*`. Examples:

## 3. Engine capabilities
- **Physics:**
  - Rapier 3D (`@dimforge/rapier3d-compat`) is wrapped in `packages/physics-rapier/src/index.ts` (851 lines). It supports box, sphere, capsule, plane, mesh, convex-hull and heightfield shapes. Body types are dynamic, fixed and kinematic. It has joints, sensors, raycasts, a character controller (`RapierCharacterControllerHandle`) and a raycast vehicle controller with wheel tuning.
  - There is also a solver-free deterministic path (`@aura3d/physics/solverless`, `PhysicsWorld.ts` at 1158 lines). `game.collisionWorld` and `game.planarCollisionWorld` handle AABB/rect/sphere/capsule colliders and triggers (`game.trigger`, `gameTriggerVolumes`).
  - The mini-game template explicitly claims no physical solver.
- **Input:**
  - `packages/input/src/` has keyboard, pointer and gamepad devices, an action map, combo detector, gesture recognizer, haptics, input replay and WebXR.
  - `VirtualTouchControls.ts` and `TouchLayouts.ts` provide a virtual joystick and touch layouts, and `game.touchControls` / `packages/game/src/touch/TouchControls.ts` wrap them. The comment says all targets are at least 48 CSS px.
  - `GameInputDeviceKind` is keyboard, pointer, touch or gamepad.
- **Audio:**
  - `packages/audio/src/game-sound/` has a sound engine, voices, spatial voice, music controller, master chain, reverb send and engine loop.
  - `assets/packs/game-sfx-core` is an SFX pack.
- **Particles / VFX:**
  - `production-runtime/effects/` has `CpuEmitter`, `EffectNodeLowering` and `ProductionEffectSystem`. `flipbook-sprite` lowers to a CPU emitter with a `flipbook {frames, frameRate, loop, columns, rows}` atlas.
  - The built-in `fireball` sheet is procedural.
  - `game.effects` and `game.effectPresets` add game-level presets. There is also WebGPU compute particles (`apps/wow-webgpu-compute-particles`).
- **2D / sprites:**
  - Everything is 3D. The renderer is WebGPU-first and WebGL-backed, with three.js-style scene nodes.
  - 2D support is partial: `packages/rendering/src/SpriteFlipbook.ts` (172 lines), `SpriteGeometry.ts` and `SdfText.ts`. The platformer and fighter kits run 2D rules on a plane.
  - I found no tilemap or Tiled loader, no Canvas2D game layer, and no 2D sprite renderer or atlas animator. Canvas2D appears only in debug and label rendering.
- **UI / HUD:**
  - `packages/game/src/hud/HudKit.ts` (413 lines) has widgets and themes. `game.hud.*` has bindings for health, score, lives, timer, combo, round, objective and checkpoint, and `nodes/ui.ts` is 103 lines.
  - HUD is DOM-based. There is also an in-world label renderer.
- **State / save:**
  - `GameSession` and lifecycle live in `packages/game/src/session/`.
  - Persistence is per-app, not an engine API. Examples are `showcase-*/src/game/save.ts` and `persistence.ts`, which use localStorage.
  - Accessibility settings (reduced motion/flash, high contrast, pause) are built in.
  - Deterministic input replay and export/import are built in.
- **Mobile:** touch layouts, haptics and context-loss recovery (`shell/contextLoss.ts`) are there. The `showcase-index` app and the game shells have touch paths.

## 4. Existing 2D/arcade assets
- `tools/asset-optimize/gen-flipbooks.py` generates flipbook sheets.
- The `aura3d-game-art` skill covers flipbook VFX sheets (`flipbook-sprite` with `spriteColumns`/`spriteRows`) and HUD icons or UI sprites as typed texture assets.
- `game/src/art/` is an art-audit and acceptance module, not an art library.
- Showcases ship SVG/PNG icons and UI SFX (`gravityPostUiConfirmSfx`).
- I found no shipped library of score sprites or HUD icons.

## 5. Gaps by game type
- **Top-down shooter:** the closest match is `templates/arena-shooter` (672 lines). It has a pooled-bolt fire loop, a spawn cadence and a shield, but nothing reusable is exposed as `game.*`.
  - Missing as kit-level pieces: enemy AI/steering, projectile pool, weapon and upgrade system, and a 2D camera or screen-space aiming helper.
  - The `navigation-recast` package exists but is 3D navmesh.
- **Tower defense:** no kit. The pieces missing are:
  - Grid or tile placement.
  - Path or waypoint following.
  - Wave scheduler.

## Cheap vs. expensive to reproduce
- **Cheap:**

## What to actually build, in order

For requests that span multiple features or subsystems, use a staged workflow:

1. Turn the request into a checklist of questions and the evidence each answer
   needs. Resolve target identity and constraints from the conversation and
   workspace before asking for information again.
2. Inspect the current REA session, artifact identity, saved analysis database,
   bookmarks, and prior evidence. Reuse matching state; do not open duplicate
   sessions or repeat identical analysis.
3. Start with the smallest useful overview or inventory. Follow each question
   from its entry point through relevant data and state changes to its result.
   Batch related operations around a specific hypothesis, then expand only when
   the returned evidence leaves a concrete gap.
4. Inspect relevant packaged resources and configuration alongside code when
   they affect the question. Use format-aware inventory and parsers; do not
   infer behavior from filenames, strings, or layout alone.
5. Corroborate a conclusion with the evidence type it requires. Use runtime
   observation only when static evidence cannot answer the question and the
   required host runtime and OS access are available. For JavaScript behavior,
   run probes against the actual app through the available browser, Electron,
   or process capture workflow.
6. Decompose work into independent questions. When parallel workers are
   available and the questions do not depend on one another, assign distinct
   scopes, point workers to existing evidence, and ask them to return sources,
   conclusions, and unresolved gaps. Otherwise, work sequentially.
7. Keep a concise finding ledger linking each conclusion to Evidence IDs,
   confidence/evidence type, search boundary, and remaining unknowns. Update
   the shared index or investigation report so later passes can reuse results.

Before finishing, revisit the original checklist. Mark each question as
answered, partially answered, or unresolved based on its evidence; keep
bounded negative searches bounded, and do not describe a broad investigation

# Skill: competitor-teardown

# Competitor Teardown & Reverse Engineering Workflow

When building a new application, vertical SaaS, prototype, or major feature—or when asked to benchmark, clone, or reverse engineer a competitor—**do not guess the domain model or UX flow from scratch.** First identify the closest best-in-class competitor, reverse engineer their live product and shipped artifacts with evidence, and use that blueprint to build a faster, denser, higher-craft version.

## Hard Rules (AuraOne Policy Alignment)

1. **Use the canonical `rea` binary (never `npx`):** `rea` (`rea-agents`) is installed globally. Always invoke `rea` directly in CLI commands or use the connected `rea` MCP server tools—never run `npx rea-agents@latest`.
2. **Keep context lean with `detail: "summary"`:** Minified bundles, `.asar` archives, and `.har` files are massive. Always start with `detail: "summary"` (MCP) or targeted projections (`inspect_analysis_view`, `trace_application_feature`, `trace_javascript_semantics`) rather than dumping raw bundles into context.
3. **Respect browser & remote execution boundaries:**
   - Interactive live browsing and login/auth flows → **Prism Browser MCP** (`prism-browser-policy`).
   - Fast API route capture & replay → **`unbrowse`**.
   - Heavy Playwright test suites or Dockerized workloads → **Remote execution** (`auraone-remote-run` / serverless CI).
4. **Never copy competitor branding or ugly UI defaults:** Reverse engineer their *architecture, data model, API contracts, state transitions, and feature mechanics*, then render our product using the **AuraOne dense UI standard** (13–14px body, 34px table rows, 32px controls, licensed fonts from `/Users/gurbakshchahal/fonts/README.md`, and the **Aurora Noir / Midnight Slate** theme).

## The 4-Stage Teardown Pipeline

### Stage 1 — Identify & Market-Map the Closest Competitor (`treg` + Search)

If the user did not name a specific competitor, identify the top 1–2 category leaders for the feature or product being built:
- Use **`treg`** (`treg catalog search` / `exa.*` / SEO & ad endpoints) or native search to identify the closest competitor, their core value proposition, pricing gates, and user complaints.
- Lock in the target URL(s) or downloadable artifact(s) (web app, Chrome extension, Electron desktop `.dmg`/`.asar`, CLI binary, or mobile `.apk`).

### Stage 2 — Capture Live UX & Active Routes (`Prism Browser` + `unbrowse`)

1. **Live UX & Flow Walkthrough (`Prism Browser MCP`):**
   - Open the competitor app via `browser_open` (`provider="auto"`).
   - Walk the critical user journey (`browser_run`, `browser_observe`) and record the exact screen sequence, navigation hierarchy, form fields, and empty/loading/error states.
2. **Fast Route Discovery (`unbrowse`):**
   - Run `unbrowse "<core action or data read>" --url "<competitor_url>"` (or `unbrowse capture`) to capture live API endpoints and response shapes.

### Stage 3 — Deep Technical Reverse Engineering (`rea`)

Use **`rea`** (MCP tools or `rea <command> --json`) to extract the internal architecture, hidden API schemas, and feature logic that surface browsing cannot see:

| Competitor Target | `rea` MCP Tool / CLI Command | What It Extracts |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Live Web App / SPA (via loopback CDP)** | `list_browser_targets` → `analyze_web_bundle` & `inspect_web_page` | Full client route table, Webpack/Vite chunk graph, REST endpoints, **tRPC procedures** (`trpc:procedure:<method>`), **GraphQL queries/mutations/subscriptions**, WebSocket message shapes, storage keys, workers, and vendor fingerprints. |
| **Downloaded Web Bundle / Chrome Extension / Electron `.asar`** | `analyze_javascript_application` (`rea analyze /abs/path --json`) | Complete static AST module graph, `package.json` entrypoints, `BrowserWindow` config, `preload.js` `contextBridge` APIs, and `ipcRenderer` ↔ `ipcMain` channel pairings without executing untrusted code. |
| **Specific Feature Logic in JS/TS/Electron** | `trace_application_feature` & `trace_javascript_semantics` | Traces a single seed (route, API path, IPC channel, string literal, or DOM event) forward/backward across modules to show exact call chains, state mutations, and validation boundaries. |
| **Network Traffic (`.har` or Fiddler `.saz`)** | `inspect_web_network_capture` (`rea inspect-web-network-capture /abs/file.har har --json`) | Offline HTTP transaction inventory plus **automatic Protobuf, gRPC, and `grpc-web` frame and field decoding** (with or without a `.proto` descriptor set). |
| **Competitor CLI / Native Desktop Binary** | `inspect_rust_binary` / `inspect_go_binary` / `open_bundle_resources` | Extracts exact Rust crate dependencies (`cargo-auditable`), Go module versions & build flags, macOS `.app` plist/asset catalogs/keyed archives, or decompiled native functions (`open_binary`). |
| **Embedded WASM or Local App Database** | `inspect_wasm_artifact` / `inspect_sqlite_database` | Decompiles `.wasm` modules to WAT and inspects glue code; extracts full table schemas and sample rows from local SQLite snapshots. |
| **Mobile App (`.apk` / Flutter / Unity)** | `inspect_android_package` / `inspect_il2cpp_metadata` | Recover Android manifest, classes, methods, incoming references, or Unity IL2CPP types/methods/string literals. |

#### Context-Safe `rea` Query Pattern
Never pull a multi-megabyte graph inline when a summary + targeted view will do:
1. Call `analyze_javascript_application` or `inspect_web_network_capture` with `detail: "summary"`.
2. Take `normalized_result.parent_evidence_id` and call `inspect_analysis_view` to page `modules`, `javascript-facts`, or `protobuf` fields.
3. Call `trace_application_feature` or `trace_javascript_semantics` on the exact endpoint, IPC channel, or route you want to replicate.

### Stage 4 — Synthesize the "Parity + Edge" Blueprint & Build

Before (or while) writing the PRD and code, synthesize the teardown into four concrete inputs:
1. **Verified Data Model & API Contracts:** Entities, property names, tRPC/GraphQL/REST routes, and payload shapes proven by `rea` Evidence IDs.
2. **State Machine & Edge Cases:** How the competitor handles optimistic updates, pagination, caching, validation, and background jobs.
3. **Stack & Library Choices:** Relevant libraries, algorithms, or protocols discovered in their bundle/binary worth adopting.
4. **Our Competitive Edge (How We Beat Them):**
   - Eliminate their multi-click friction or slow round-trips.
   - Replace bloated, low-density screens with our **Aurora Noir / Midnight Slate** high-density interface and licensed typography.
   - Ship the complete vertical slice (schema + backend routes + dense UI + verification).

# Aura3D

> Aura3D: AI-Native TypeScript 3D SDK for Browser 3D Apps — typed scenes, looks, typed GLB/glTF assets, camera rigs, gameFeel, and gameplay through `@aura3d/engine` plus the `@aura3d/cli` toolchain, for browser 3D apps and interactive websites.

Aura3D is the AI-native TypeScript 3D SDK for browser 3D apps, interactive websites, prompt-to-code scene kits, typed GLB/glTF assets, Vite templates, diagnostics, screenshots, and static deploy checks.

## Facts

- Product: AI-native TypeScript 3D SDK for browser 3D apps, interactive websites, and prompt-to-code scene kits
- Website: https://aura3d.auraone.ai
- Current release: Aura3D 4.0.3 (per the repo manifest — the same source the build's version guard uses)
- Docs: https://aura3d.auraone.ai/docs/api.html
- Showcase game: https://aura3d.auraone.ai/showcase/aura-clash/
- Sitemap: https://aura3d.auraone.ai/sitemap.xml
- Crawl policy: https://aura3d.auraone.ai/robots.txt (public content allow-all; build internals and source maps disallowed)
- Last updated: 2026-10-20

## Pages

- [Home](https://aura3d.auraone.ai/): Aura3D is the AI-native TypeScript 3D SDK for browser 3D apps, interactive websites, prompt-to-code scene kits, typed GLB/glTF assets, Vite templates, diagnostics, screenshots, and static deploy checks.

### Docs

- [Aura3D Agent Quickstart for TypeScript 3D Apps](https://aura3d.auraone.ai/docs/agent-quickstart.html): Create an Aura3D browser 3D app with Vite, scene kits, typed assets, diagnostics, and AI-assisted TypeScript development.
- [Aura3D Agent Setup for AI Coding Assistants](https://aura3d.auraone.ai/docs/agent-rules.html): Set up AI coding assistants to generate Aura3D TypeScript scenes with public SDK imports, scene kits, primitives, typed assets, and Vite templates.
- [Aura3D TypeScript API for Agent-Written 3D Scenes](https://aura3d.auraone.ai/docs/api.html): Aura3D TypeScript API overview for scenes, models, cameras, lights, materials, primitives, scene kits, interactions, diagnostics, screenshots, and typed assets.

=== game-example-standards (head) ===
# Game Example Standards

Use this when building or reviewing Aura3D game examples.

Read `llms.txt`, `docs/agents/claims-and-boundaries.md`, and
`docs/api/game-runtime.md` first. A route with a scene, keyboard listener, or
proof replay is not automatically a game.

## Minimum Public Game Standard

A public game example must prove:

- player input visibly changes game state;
- reset works after normal play and after win/fail where applicable;
- there is a clear objective;
- there is scoring, timing, progress, or a fail condition;
- there is at least one real progression loop;
- primary character, vehicle, playfield, world, or track assets are typed
  GLB/glTF assets unless the game is explicitly abstract;
- route-health names renderer mode, fallback state, exact primary assets,
  primitive count, known limits, and claims;
- automated browser tests cover movement, restart, and at least one win, fail,
  score, lap, checkpoint, line-clear, collection, or completion mechanic;
- screenshots show first load, after input, mid-route, fail/reset when relevant,
  and finish/progression;
- the visual bar: the genre's look preset is applied (see
  `docs/agents/art-direction.md`), the frame shows environment light, a full
  key shadow, genre palette and fog/grade from the look — a mechanic-correct
  game on flat lighting and a void background is still `prototype`.
- all current release, visual-QA, and deploy gates for that exact route pass;
  historical retained evidence cannot override a failing current gate.

## Session Length

Showcase games must not be five-to-ten-second micro demos. For prompt recovery
work, a game route must support at least 60 seconds of meaningful play evidence
before it can be called a public game candidate. A short deterministic proof may
supplement the evidence, but it does not replace player-driven playability.

If the current public game kit cannot support that standard, mark the route
`prototype` and add a library task instead of hiding the gap in route code.

## Genre Standards

### Racing

Required:

- manual throttle/brake/steer;
- car starts on a readable track;
- camera keeps car and route readable;
- ordered checkpoints;
- lap or finish progression;
- penalty, fail, timeout, or bounded no-fail claim;
- reset after finish/fail;

=== game-showcase-build (head) ===
# Aura Clash Arena Showcase Build Guide

Version: 4.0.0

Use this guide when editing, reviewing, or documenting the active Aura3D game showcase in `apps/aura-clash-showcase`.

Aura Clash Arena is the current browser-game development showcase for Aura3D.
It exercises a scoped runtime foundation across root and lower-level Aura3D
package surfaces: typed GLB assets, a game lifecycle, input, animation state,
engine combat evidence, HUD updates, screenshots, deployment checks, and
npm/CLI proof. It is not blanket root `createAuraApp` or flagship-quality
evidence.

It is a development showcase built with starter-grade fighter assets, focused on proving the engine's runtime, animation, and combat systems.

## Non-Negotiables

- Read `llms.txt` before authoring Aura3D code.
- Use public imports from `@aura3d/engine`.
- Use one app/runtime owner per route through the current public game-runtime path.
- Use typed assets from `src/aura-assets.ts`; never pass string asset ids, invented GLB URLs, raw loaders, or direct Three.js imports.
- Use the asset catalog profile for fighter prompts:

```bash
npx @aura3d/cli@latest assets search "animated humanoid fighting character" --profile fighting-character --json
npx @aura3d/cli@latest assets resolve "animated humanoid fighting character" --name fighter --profile fighting-character
npx @aura3d/cli@latest assets validate-game --profile fighting-character --asset auraClashPlayerRig --asset auraClashRivalRig --no-placeholders --require-license
```

- If the catalog returns no production-ready candidate, stop and report the rejection reasons. Do not force a static prop, aircraft, spider, unlicensed sculpt, or broken-scale model into a fighter slot.
- Do not use primitives as release-facing fighter art. Primitives are allowed for set dressing, debug modes, and deterministic tests only.
- Hide hitboxes, boxes, line artifacts, and debug rigs in normal play. Debug visuals must be behind an explicit debug/evidence mode.
- Keep public copy scoped to "development showcase" and "runtime proof" until gameplay, asset, art, audio, performance, deployment, and visual approval gates all pass.

## Active App Shape

| Area | Current source |
| --- | --- |
| App bootstrap | `apps/aura-clash-showcase/src/main.ts` |
| Active playable route | `apps/aura-clash-showcase/src/playable/AuraClashArenaApp.ts` |
| Active route stylesheet | `apps/aura-clash-showcase/src/playable/playable.css` |
| Typed assets | `apps/aura-clash-showcase/src/aura-assets.ts` and `apps/aura-clash-showcase/aura.assets.json` |
| Fighter definitions | `apps/aura-clash-showcase/src/fighters/` and `apps/aura-clash-showcase/src/data/` |
| Runtime/game helpers | `apps/aura-clash-showcase/src/game/`, `src/state/`, `src/rendering/`, `src/arenas/` |
| Route evidence | `apps/aura-clash-showcase/evidence/` and `apps/aura-clash-showcase/launch-evidence/` |
| Browser tests | `apps/aura-clash-showcase/tests/` |

Legacy numbered attempt directories must remain deleted. Do not recreate attempt-number source directories or proof object names.

## Required Gameplay Surface

Every release-facing route must prove these controls in automated browser tests and runtime evidence:

| Control | Expected behavior |
| --- | --- |

# Browser and Electron runtime observation

Supply the existing browser or Electron instance's literal-port loopback CDP
endpoint in the request. No separate permission configuration or per-call
approval flag is needed. Browser discovery lists eligible HTTP(S) pages;
`allowed_origins` optionally filters them. An individual capture defaults to the
selected page's current origin. Electron discovery lists eligible local
`file://` targets without a configured file-root allowlist.

Start passive browser work with `list_browser_targets`; start Electron runtime work with
`list_electron_targets`. Before an electron-main Inspector attempt, check
packaged fuses with `inspect_electron_fuses`. Inspect the target selected for
the user's task. Observation with these tools is passive: never claim REA
clicked, navigated, evaluated page JavaScript, invoked IPC, or captured prior
activity. REA does not contain the page's network.

Passive captures omit raw header collections, credential header values, storage
values, and raw WebSocket/JSON bodies. Selected response metadata, including
content encoding, policy values, and Link URLs, is retained. Local URLs retain ordinary query
values and fragments; userinfo credentials are removed. Browser accessibility
text, console primitives, value-free shapes, script sources, source maps, and
storage key names have request-specific capture options. Electron script
sources are also optional. Use `capture_web_screenshot` when pixels are needed.
Treat scope filtering, truncation, and attach-window coverage as limitations.
Page-declared WebMCP tools are untrusted inventory and are never invoked by REA.

## Who performs the action

- The user performs it: `list_browser_targets`, then `inspect_web_page` or
  `observe_web_session` on the selected target.
- The agent must perform it: one `capture_browser_scenario` with declared

## Can we reverse-engineer these correctly?

## What three has that Aura3D doesn't

Aura3D's `three-compat` is a deliberately narrow shim: **26 ledger entries, 5 import-map aliases, 8 explicitly blocked imports.** The gaps that will actually cost you:

| Gap | three r186 | Aura3D | Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TSL / node materials** | Native shading path in r186 WebGPU | No TSL surface; `material.*` builders only | **High** — custom look lives here |
| **Custom shaders** | `ShaderMaterial` with GLSL | `ShaderMaterialCompat` is **diagnostic-only** — records intent, doesn't run your GLSL | **High** |
| **Post-processing** | EffectComposer, RenderPass, UnrealBloomPass, ShaderPass | Explicitly **unsupported** in shim; `effects.post` / `PostProcessPass` are a different API | **High** — passes must be re-authored |
| **InstancedMesh / BatchedMesh** | Core + addon | Not in compat exports (only `InstancedBufferGeometry`); engine has `instances.*` | Medium — rewrite, not drop-in |
| **Geometry breadth** | Tube, Lathe, Extrude, Shape, TorusKnot, Capsule | 9 geometry types, none of those | Medium |
| **Math breadth** | Vector2/4, Euler, Box3, Sphere, Ray, Matrix3, Curve | Only Vector3, Quaternion, Matrix4, Color | Medium |
| **Loaders** | GLTF/KTX2/EXR/OBJ/MTL | All **diagnostic-only** — typed assets required | Low, but every asset must be re-registered |
| **Fog / Clock / Audio** | Fog, FogExp2, Clock, PositionalAudio | Look-based fog, runtime timing, `@aura3d/audio` | Low |
| **Version skew** | r186 | Ledger is written against **r185** (`deltaVsR185`) | Low |

The important pattern: the gaps cluster exactly where a game's **visual identity** lives — shaders, node materials, post stacks. Geometry and math gaps are mechanical; shader gaps are authoring work.

## What is not a problem

Renderer family (both WebGPU), physics (**Rapier 0.12 on both sides**), skinning/animation (faithful shims), controls (8 faithful), lights (5 faithful, spot/rect-area approximated), the game kits, HUD, touch, audio. Fetching and running the games is a solved problem; the flow proves it.

## What this means per game

- **Strange Orbit (19 KB), Splat Rush (43 KB), Cube Dash (21 KB)** — small, almost certainly no custom post stack. Port cleanly and cheaply. Start here.
- **HEATSINK (1.64 MB), Drift & Deliver, Last Train** — big bundles, weather/rain/heat imagery. Assume custom node materials and post passes; budget a look-dev pass, not just a mechanics pass.
- **Ninja Runner (4,447 lines)** — most readable; best one to trace semantically.

The honest bottom line: **you can reverse-engineer all ten correctly and cheaply. Running them is not the hard part — reproducing their look is**, because that's concentrated in TSL and custom post passes, and Aura3D has no mechanical bridge for either. Plan for "extract mechanics + tuning, rebuild the look with `material.*` / `looks` / `effects.post`", not "port the shader".

75: 
76: ---
77: 
78: ## 2. The flow
79: 
80: Seven stages. Stages 1–4 are REA; stages 5–7 are Aura3D.
81: 
82: ### Stage 0 — Prerequisites
83: 
84: ```bash
85: rea --version                      # expect 6.7.0
86: "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" \
87:   --headless=new --remote-debugging-port=9222 \
88:   --user-data-dir="$TMPDIR/crayon-chrome" --no-first-run \
89:   "https://app.usecrayon.ai/play/<project_id>" &
90: ```
91: 
92: REA only accepts loopback: `http://127.0.0.1:9222` or the `ws://` browser URL.
93: A Docker or remote browser will not work — the endpoint must be on this machine.
94: 
95: ### Stage 1 — Discover targets
96: 
97: ```bash
98: rea list-browser-targets http://127.0.0.1:9222 \
99:   --allowed-origins https://app.usecrayon.ai --format json
100: ```
101: 
102: You will see the `page` (the shell) **and** an `iframe` with `about:srcdoc`.
103: Note both IDs.
104: 
105: ### Stage 2 — Capture the frame, not the page
106: 
107: ```bash
108: NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192 \
109: rea analyze-web-bundle http://127.0.0.1:9222 <iframe_target_id> \
110:   --allowed-origins https://app.usecrayon.ai \
111:   --allowed-origins https://api.usecrayon.ai \
112:   --observation-ms 3000 --format json > frame.json
113: ```
114: 
115: Targeting the **frame** keeps the bundle at 120–320 KB instead of 1.34 MB. This
116: single choice is the difference between a 45-second run and a crash.
117: 
118: ### Stage 3 — Extract the game unit
119: 
120: Three shapes occur. Handle all three or you will silently get 0 bytes:
121: 
122: 1. **External blob module** — `<script type="module" src="blob:...">`. Fetch the
123:    blob inside the frame's own JS context and write the text out.
124: 2. **Inline module** — no `src`; read `textContent`.
125: 3. **Dynamic import** — no script element and no blob entry in
126:    `performance.getEntriesByType("resource")`. The DOM probe returns nothing.
127:    Use Stage 2's CDP script enumeration (`analyze-web-bundle` lists scripts from
128:    the debugger, including blob/data/inline) or `rea export-web-scripts`.
129: 
130: Also record the frame's `importmap` — it is the stack fingerprint and the exact
131: dependency pin.
132: 
133: ### Stage 4 — Static semantics
134: 
135: ```bash
136: rea export-web-scripts /abs/frame.json /abs/game-scripts      # absent dir
137: rea analyze-javascript-application /abs/game-scripts --json   # module graph
138: rea trace-javascript-semantics '<workflow json>'               # see --schema
139: ```
140: 
141: Trace **seeds**, not whole files. For the racing games the productive seeds are
142: `overheat`, `checkpoint`, `lap`, `traffic`, `boost`, `trafficSpawn`, `HUD`.
143: For runners: `gate`, `speed`, `jump`, `spawn`, `score`.
144: 
145: `analyze-javascript-application` defaults to a 1024 MiB analyzer heap. Raise it:
146: 
147: ```bash
148: rea analyze-javascript-application /abs/game-scripts \
149:   --max-heap-mb 4096 --max-semantic-nodes 200000 --json
150: ```
151: 
152: ### Stage 5 — Build a parity fixture (not a screenshot)
153: 
154: One declared scenario, capture the input → state transition:
155: 
156: ```bash
157: rea capture-browser-scenario /abs/scenario.json --format json > before.json
158: ```
159: 
160: Connect mode navigates to `start_url` and runs declared actions. Capture again
161: after the Aura3D port, then diff:
162: 
163: ```bash
164: rea compare-web-captures before.json after.json --format json
165: ```
166: 
167: Comparison is normalized (step timing, event sequence, and local network IDs are
168: ignored) and reports per-artifact diffs. This is the closest thing to a
169: mechanical parity gate and it is the only stage that proves *behaviour* rather
170: than structure.
171: 
172: ### Stage 6 — Map to Aura3D
173: 
174: | Crayon mechanic | Aura3D surface | Status |
175: | --- | --- | --- |
176: | Vehicle + track + laps | `game.racing`, `game.arcadeKart` | ships |
177: | Combat + projectiles | `templates/arena-shooter` pooled-bolt pattern | template, not a kit |
178: | Heat / resource meter | `game.simulation` state + HUD binding | compose |
179: | Drift scoring | arcade kart velocity model | compose |
180: | Traffic / AI | racing kit AI + spawner | compose |
181: | Endless runner lanes | `game.platformer` + `game.planarCollisionWorld` | **no runner kit** |
182: | 3D collect / wander | `game.locomotion` + character controller | compose |
183: | HUD / score / lives | `packages/game/src/hud/HudKit.ts` | ships |
184: | Touch controls | `game.touchControls` | ships |
185: | VFX | `effects.flipbook` | ships |
186: 
187: ### Stage 7 — Prove it
188: 
189: Nothing is "done" on a screenshot. The repo gate is
190: `docs/agents/game-example-standards.md`:
191: 
192: - input visibly changes state; reset works after win and fail;
193: - objective + scoring/timing/progress/fail;
194: - at least one progression loop;
195: - ≥60 s of meaningful player-driven play;
196: - typed GLB for primary character/vehicle/track, not primitives;
197: - genre look preset applied (a mechanic-correct game on flat lighting is still
198:   `prototype`);
199: - route-health names renderer mode, fallback, primary assets, primitive count,
200:   known limits;
201: - browser tests cover movement, restart, and one win/fail/score/lap/completion.
202: 
203: ```bash
204: pnpm -C packages/aura3d-cli aura3d assets validate-game --profile <genre> \
205:   --asset <key> --no-placeholders --require-license
206: pnpm game-runtime:unit && pnpm game-runtime:browser
207: pnpm check:release
208: ```
209: 
210: ---
211: 
212: ## 3. Known failure modes (all hit during validation)
213: 
214: | Symptom | Cause | Fix |
215: | --- | --- | --- |
216: | MCP `analyze_web_bundle` → *"MCP server process exited"*, V8 stack | 1.34 MB minified AST exceeds the server's heap and the MCP transport | Use the CLI, not MCP |
217: | CLI exit 134, `Scavenge ... 4080 MB` | 4 GB default heap | `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192` (peak observed 7.3 GB) |
218: | 45 s → 0-byte output | Same OOM, output truncated | same |
219: | `403 client_not_allowed` | Origin gate on `api.usecrayon.ai` | Browser context only; never curl |
220: | Module extract returns 0 bytes | Dynamic import, no DOM script, no blob perf entry | Stage 2 CDP enumeration |
221: | `source_maps: not_requested`, no maps found | Publisher ships none | Drop `--fetch-source-maps` |
222: 
223: ---
224: 
225: ## 4. Legal and claim boundaries
226: 
227: - Reproduce **mechanics, systems, tuning, and control contracts**. Do not copy
228:   art, audio, text, names, or branding. All assets come from the Aura3D catalog
229:   with `--require-license`.
230: - Do not describe a port as "1:1" unless the parity fixture in Stage 5 passes
231:   and the route-health entry names the exact limits.
232: - `apps/showcase-heatsink` and `apps/showcase-roadster-rush` are **not** Crayon
233:   ports. The Roadster showcase documents a different source
234:   (`roadster-rush.ai.studio`); `showcase-heatsink` has no provenance note. The
235:   name overlap with Crayon's *HEATSINK* / *Roadster Hours* is coincidence.
236:   Do not cite them as prior parity work.
237: 
238: ---
239: 
240: ## 5. Recommended order
241: 
242: 1. **Strange Orbit** (19,300 B) — smallest module in the set, full racing kit
243:    coverage. Cheapest end-to-end proof that the whole seven-stage flow works.
244: 2. **HEATSINK** (1.64 MB) — highest demand × best kit fit; adds weapons + heat.
245: 3. **Splat Rush** (43,212 B) — cheapest retention loop; one-button + colour gates.
246: 4. **Ninja Runner** (867 KB, 4,447 lines) — most readable module; runner + combat
247:    + forms; forces the runner kit decision.
248: 5. **Last Train to the Sea** (1.39 MB) — the catalog's #1 game and the showcase
249:    bet; needs a vehicle-adventure kit that does not exist yet.
````

3: Validated flow for the ten candidate games from `app.usecrayon.ai`, using REA 6.7.0

7: Nothing here is inferred from filenames or marketing copy.
8: 
9: **Two documents, one pipeline.**
10:

20: 
21: ## 1. What the target actually is
22: 
23: Crayon is **not** a single SPA whose bundle contains the games. There are three
24: layers, and only the last one matters:
25: 
26: | Layer | What it is | Size | Do we care |
27: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
28: | Shell | React SPA at `app.usecrayon.ai` (`index`, `vendor`, `core`, `messageRouter`, `levelOverrides`, `uiContext`, `engineBrand`, `restoreVersion` chunks) | 1.34 MB + 1.37 MB + 298 KB | **No** — this is what blows up analyzers |
29: | Game frame | `<iframe data-game-preview sandbox srcdoc>` titled **"Play Labs runtime"** | 120 KB – 317 KB | Yes — it is the game's document |
30: | Game module | `<script type="module" src="blob:...">`, or inline, or dynamic import | 19 KB – 1.64 MB | **Yes — this is the source** |
31: 
32: The dependency manifest is published in the frame's `importmap`. It is identical
33: for **all twelve** games measured:
34: 
35: ```
36: three                            -> cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.184.0/build/three.module.min.js
37: three/addons/                    -> .../three@0.184.0/examples/jsm/
38: @dimforge/rapier3d-compat        -> .../rapier3d-compat@0.12.0/rapier.es.js
39: ```
40: 
41: **The importmap is not what renders.** On the live HEATSINK frame:
42: 
43: ```
44: window.__THREE__      = "184"                      // the importmap copy
45: canvas[data-engine]   = "three.js r186 webgpu"     // the renderer actually drawing
46: ```
47: 
48: Only `WebGPURenderer` writes that `data-engine` string. So the real stack is
49: **three r186 WebGPU, bundled inside the game module**, coexisting with an unused
50: r184 global. Two consequences:
51: 
52: - A `THREE.*` shim will never be a drop-in: the game does not call the global.
53: - Aura3D is also WebGPU-first, so the renderer family matches even though the
54:   versions do not. The gap is authoring surface, not backend.
55: 
56: Other facts that shape the flow:
57: 
58: - **Module size tells you the extraction method.** A minified three build is
59:   365 KB (`three.module.min.js`) and the WebGPU build is 668 KB. A 19 KB module
60:   cannot contain either, so small modules import through the importmap and stay
61:   readable. Modules above ~500 KB inline their own renderer and are minified
62:   end-to-end: `new Mesh(` returns **0 matches** in HEATSINK.
63: - **Game-domain names survive; library names do not.** HEATSINK carries
64:   `overheat` ×15, `drone` ×280, `HUD` ×316, `checkpoint` ×25, `lap` ×70 — because
65:   they are object properties. `WebGPURenderer` ×12 and `BatchedMesh` ×12 are
66:   library definitions, not proof that the game uses them. Trace, don't grep.
67: - No source maps are published (`sourceMappingURL` absent from every chunk), so
68:   `--fetch-source-maps` buys nothing.
69: 
70: ### The public API is origin-gated
71: 
72: ```
73: GET https://api.usecrayon.ai/play/<project_id>
74: HTTP/2 403
75: {"error":"client_not_allowed","message":"This content can only be opened in the Crayon app."}
76: ```
77: 
78: The same request succeeds **inside the browser page**. So never `curl` the game
79: payload; every read goes through a real browser context. This is why REA's
80: loopback-CDP provider is the correct tool and why REA refuses non-loopback
81: endpoints by design.

251: ## 3. Known failure modes (all hit during validation)
252: 
253: | Symptom | Cause | Fix |
254: | --- | --- | --- |
255: | MCP `analyze_web_bundle` → *"MCP server process exited"*, V8 stack | 1.34 MB minified AST exceeds the server's heap and the MCP transport | Use the CLI, not MCP |
256: | CLI exit 134, `Scavenge ... 4080 MB` | 4 GB default heap | `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192` (peak observed 7.3 GB) |
257: | 45 s → 0-byte output | Same OOM, output truncated | same |
258: | `403 client_not_allowed` | Origin gate on `api.usecrayon.ai` | Browser context only; never curl |
259: | Module extract returns 0 bytes | Dynamic import, no DOM script, no blob perf entry | Stage 2 CDP enumeration |
260: | `source_maps: not_requested`, no maps found | Publisher ships none | Drop `--fetch-source-maps` |

264: ## 4. Legal and claim boundaries
265: 
266: - Reproduce **mechanics, systems, tuning, and control contracts**. Do not copy
267:   art, audio, text, names, or branding. All assets come from the Aura3D catalog
268:   with `--require-license`.
269: - Do not describe a port as "1:1" unless the parity fixture in Stage 5 passes
270:   and the route-health entry names the exact limits.
271: - `apps/showcase-heatsink` and `apps/showcase-roadster-rush` are **not** Crayon
272:   ports. The Roadster showcase documents a different source
273:   (`roadster-rush.ai.studio`); `showcase-heatsink` has no provenance note. The
274:   name overlap with Crayon's *HEATSINK* / *Roadster Hours* is coincidence.
275:   Do not cite them as prior parity work.
276:

282: gate is:
283: 
284: | Tier | Items | Meaning |
285: | --- | --- | --- |
286: | **P0** | SH-02 custom shaders, SH-03 custom pass, SG-03 geometry breadth, SG-05 geometry authoring, SM-01 math, SM-02 curves, ST-01/02 textures | No port can look like the source without these |
287: | **P1** | SH-01 TSL subset, SH-05 renderer facade, SH-07 PMREM, SG-01/02 instancing, SG-06/07 lines/points, SA-01/04 animation, AU-01/02/04 audio, SR-01/02/05/08 | Required by at least one title |
288: | **P2** | WebXR, CubeCamera, exporters, CSM, full addon ecosystem | Does not block the ten |
289: 
290: A game starts only when every item marked `●` in the parity matrix has a passing
291: fixture. "Mechanically correct, visually prototype" is the failure mode this gate
292: exists to prevent.

- inspect_managed_members(`path?`: `string`, `detail?`: `string`, `type_names?`: `array`): Inspect PE/CLI metadata members, signatures, raw CIL hashes, decoded-instruction-tuple hashes, separately reported exception regions, call edges, field-access anchors, and the #US string literals that ldstr loads, without loading or executing target code.
- inspect_managed_native_boundaries(`path?`: `string`): Inspect PE/CLI ModuleRef, ImplMap/PInvoke declarations, CLI native-header indicators, and non-IL method implementation flags without loading or executing target code.

### Stage 5 — Build a parity fixture (observable, not internal)

REA has two capture surfaces and they are not interchangeable:

| Artifact | Produced by | Passed to compare as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Passive inspection | `inspect-web-page` | `before` / `after` (`{ inspection }`) |
| Controlled scenario | `capture-browser-scenario` | `before_scenario` / `after_scenario` |
| Screenshot | `capture-web-screenshot` | `compare-web-screenshots` |

`compare-web-captures` does not take scenario JSON in `before`/`after`; those
slots require an inspection with a `target`, `dom`, `accessibility`, `scripts`,
`network`, `console`, and `storage`. A scenario record goes in
`before_scenario`/`after_scenario`. Passing the wrong one fails validation.

Minimal scenario (exact fields from the 6.7.0 schema):

```json
{
  "browser": { "mode": "connect", "cdp_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:9222", "target_id": "<page-id>" },
  "start_url": { "url": "https://app.usecrayon.ai/play/<id>" },
  "actions": [
    { "step_id": "wait-boot", "action": "wait_for_timeout", "duration_ms": 2500 },
    { "step_id": "press-throttle", "action": "press", "locator": { "kind": "css", "selector": "body" }, "key": "KeyW" }
  ],
  "capture": {
    "after_each_step": ["screenshot", "url"],
    "at_end": ["screenshot", "dom", "accessibility", "storage"],
    "events": ["console", "page-errors", "network"]
  }
}
```

Locator kinds: `test_id` (`value`), `role` (`role` + `name`), `css` (`selector`).
Actions: `goto`, `click`, `fill`, `press`, `select_option`, `check`/`uncheck`,
`wait_for`, `wait_for_timeout`. Capture sections: `screenshot`, `dom`,
`accessibility`, `url`, `history`, `storage`.

**The frame is outside this surface.** REA rejects `about:srcdoc` targets, so
scenario locators only reach the shell page. For in-frame input (throttle, jump,
steer) drive the iframe session directly with `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` /
`Input.dispatchMouseEvent`, or use Playwright with `frameLocator`. Treat the REA
scenario as the shell-level fixture (load, start, pause, restart) and the raw CDP
script as the in-game fixture.

**Assert only what is observable.** REA does not evaluate JavaScript, so a
fixture cannot read `lap`, `heat`, or `pickupCount` from game memory. It can read
HUD text through DOM/accessibility, the URL, storage, console events, and pixels.

const CDP = "http://127.0.0.1:9222";

if (!frame) throw new Error("no srcdoc frame");
const ws = new WebSocket(frame.webSocketDebuggerUrl);
let seq = 0;
const pending = new Map();
ws.onmessage = e => {
  const m = JSON.parse(e.data);
  if (pending.has(m.id)) { pending.get(m.id)(m); pending.delete(m.id); }
};
const send = (method, params) => new Promise(resolve => {
  const id = ++seq; pending.set(id, resolve);
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ id, method, params }));
});
await new Promise(resolve => { ws.onopen = resolve; });
await send("Runtime.enable", {});

    const scripts = [...document.querySelectorAll('script[type="module"]')];
    const out = [];
    for (const s of scripts) {
      let text = null;
      if (s.src.startsWith('blob:')) {
        try { text = await (await fetch(s.src)).text(); } catch {}
      }
      out.push({ src: s.src || null, inlineBytes: s.textContent.length,
                 blobBytes: text ? text.length : null, sample: text?.slice(0, 160) });
    }
    const blobs = performance.getEntriesByType('resource')
      .map(r => r.name).filter(n => n.startsWith('blob:'));
    return JSON.stringify({ title: document.title, scripts: out, blobs });
  })()`
});
console.log(result.result.value);
ws.close();
```

REA has two capture surfaces and they are not interchangeable:

| Artifact | Produced by | Compare slot (MCP) |

| Passive inspection (`dom`, `accessibility`, `scripts`, `network`, `console`, `storage`) | `inspect-web-page` | `before.inspection` / `after.inspection` |
| Controlled scenario (`steps`, `events`, `completeness`) | `capture-browser-scenario` | `before_scenario` / `after_scenario` |
| Screenshot artifact | `capture-web-screenshot` | `compare-web-screenshots` |

`compare-web-captures` takes both in one call at the MCP layer; the CLI takes two
positional files and detects the shape. Do not put a scenario record where an
inspection is expected — the `inspection` object must contain `target`, `dom`,
`accessibility`, `scripts`, `network`, `console`, and `storage`.

    "at_end": ["screenshot", "dom", "accessibility", "storage"],
    "events": ["console", "page-errors", "network"]
  }
}
```

`wait_for`, `wait_for_timeout`.
Capture sections: `screenshot`, `dom`, `accessibility`, `url`, `history`, `storage`.

**The frame is outside this surface.** The scenario schema has no frame selector,
and `about:srcdoc` targets are rejected. Locator actions run on the shell page;
keyboard events reach whatever is focused but cannot be aimed at a frame element.
Drive in-game input through the iframe session with `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` /
`Input.dispatchMouseEvent`, or Playwright's `frameLocator`. Treat the REA scenario
as the shell-level fixture (load, start, pause, restart) and the raw CDP script
as the in-game fixture.

**Assert only what is observable.** REA does not evaluate JavaScript, so a
fixture cannot read `lap`, `heat`, or `pickupCount` from game memory. It can read
HUD text via DOM/accessibility, the URL, storage, console events, and pixels.
Write acceptance as "HUD shows `LAP 2/7`", not "lap === 2".

123: 
124: REA only accepts loopback: `http://127.0.0.1:9222` or the `ws://` browser URL.
125: A Docker or remote browser will not work — the endpoint must be on this machine.
126: 
127: ### Stage 1 — Discover targets (raw CDP, not REA)
128: 
129: REA's browser tools accept only HTTP(S) page targets inside an allowed origin.
130: `about:srcdoc` is rejected with `target_unavailable` / `target_not_allowed` by
131: `list-browser-targets`, `analyze-web-bundle`, `inspect-web-page`, and
132: `capture-web-screenshot` — CLI and MCP alike. Discovery of the game frame is raw
133: CDP:
134: 
135: ```bash
136: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/list | node -e 'let s="";
137: process.stdin.on("data",d=>s+=d).on("end",()=>{
138:   for (const t of JSON.parse(s)) console.log(t.type, t.id, t.url);
139: })'
140: ```
141: 
142: You will see a `page` with the app URL and an `iframe` with `about:srcdoc`. Keep
143: the iframe ID — that is the game. REA is then used on the **page** (captures,
144: scenarios, screenshots) and on **local files** (static analysis). It never touches
145: the frame.
146: 
147: ### Stage 2 — Extract from the frame (CDP evaluate)
148: 
149: `analyze-web-bundle` cannot see the frame, and running it on the page analyzes the
150: shell: in the recorded HEATSINK capture `target_url` is the app page,
151: `scripts_observed` is 11, and the largest script is **1,372,740 B**. That is the
152: vendor chunk — the 1.34 MB analyzer workload, and the OOM. It contains no game
153: code.
154: 
155: Attach to the iframe target and evaluate in its own context:
156: 
157: ```js
158: // probe.mjs — Node 18+, no dependencies
159: const CDP = "http://127.0.0.1:9222";
160: const list = await (await fetch(`${CDP}/json/list`)).json();
161: const frame = list.find(t => t.type === "iframe" && t.url === "about:srcdoc");
162: if (!frame) throw new Error("no srcdoc frame");
163: const ws = new WebSocket(frame.webSocketDebuggerUrl);
164: let seq = 0;
165: const pending = new Map();
166: ws.onmessage = e => {
167:   const m = JSON.parse(e.data);
168:   if (pending.has(m.id)) { pending.get(m.id)(m); pending.delete(m.id); }
169: };
170: const send = (method, params) => new Promise(resolve => {
171:   const id = ++seq; pending.set(id, resolve);
172:   ws.send(JSON.stringify({ id, method, params }));
173: });
174: await new Promise(resolve => { ws.onopen = resolve; });
175: await send("Runtime.enable", {});
176: const { result } = await send("Runtime.evaluate", {
177:   awaitPromise: true, returnByValue: true,
178:   expression: `(async () => {
179:     const scripts = [...document.querySelectorAll('script[type="module"]')];
180:     const out = [];
181:     for (const s of scripts) {
182:       let text = null;
183:       if (s.src.startsWith('blob:')) {
184:         try { text = await (await fetch(s.src)).text(); } catch {}
185:       }
186:       out.push({ src: s.src || null, inlineBytes: s.textContent.length,
187:                  blobBytes: text ? text.length : null, sample: text?.slice(0, 160) });
188:     }
189:     const blobs = performance.getEntriesByType('resource')
190:       .map(r => r.name).filter(n => n.startsWith('blob:'));
191:     return JSON.stringify({ title: document.title, scripts: out, blobs });
192:   })()`
193: });
194: console.log(result.result.value);
195: ws.close();
196: ```
197: 
198: Run it, then fetch the chosen blob inside the same context and write the text to
199: `game-module.mjs`. Returning 1.6 MB through `Runtime.evaluate` is fine.
200: 
201: ### Stage 3 — Classify the module
202: 
203: Three shapes occur. Handle all three or you will silently get 0 bytes:
204: 
205: 1. **External blob module** — `<script type="module" src="blob:...">`. Fetch it
206:    inside the frame (Stage 2). Nine of the twelve measured games.
207: 2. **Inline module** — no `src`; read `textContent`.
208: 3. **Dynamic import** — no script element and no blob resource entry.
209:    `analyze-web-bundle` cannot help (it cannot see the frame). Enable
210:    `Debugger.enable` + `Runtime.enable` on the iframe session and collect
211:    `Debugger.scriptParsed` events while the game boots; the module appears as a
212:    `blob:` or `data:` script URL. Fetch that URL from the page context.
213: 
214: Also record the frame's `importmap` — it is the stack fingerprint, but not proof
215: of what actually renders (see §1).
216: 
217: While the frame is still open, run the four runtime probes in
218: [`threejs-parity-gaps.md`](../../../workflows/threejs-parity-gaps.md) §9: node-material usage,
219: `BatchedMesh`, `EffectComposer`, and GLSL `ShaderMaterial`. They need
220: `Runtime.evaluate` on the iframe session — REA is passive by contract and cannot
221: do this. One session per game answers all four and decides whether SH-01 and
222: SH-02 are really P0 for that title.
223: 
224: ### Stage 4 — Static semantics
225: 
226: ```bash
227: rea export-web-scripts /abs/frame.json /abs/game-scripts      # absent dir
228: rea analyze-javascript-application /abs/game-scripts --json   # module graph
229: rea trace-javascript-semantics '<workflow json>'               # see --schema
230: ```
231: 
232: Trace **seeds**, not whole files. For the racing games the productive seeds are
233: `overheat`, `checkpoint`, `lap`, `traffic`, `boost`, `trafficSpawn`, `HUD`.
234: For runners: `gate`, `speed`, `jump`, `spawn`, `score`.
235: 
236: `analyze-javascript-application` defaults to a 1024 MiB analyzer heap. Raise it:
237: 
238: ```bash
239: rea analyze-javascript-application /abs/game-scripts \
240:   --max-heap-mb 4096 --max-semantic-nodes 200000 --json
241: ```
242: 
243: ### Stage 5 — Build a parity fixture (not a screenshot)
244: 
245: One declared scenario, capture the input → state transition:
246: 
247: ```bash
248: rea capture-browser-scenario /abs/scenario.json --format json > before.json
249: ```
250: 
251: Connect mode navigates to `start_url` and runs declared actions. Capture again
252: after the Aura3D port, then diff:
253: 
254: ```bash
255: rea compare-web-captures before.json after.json --format json
256: ```
257: 
258: Comparison is normalized (step timing, event sequence, and local network IDs are
259: ignored) and reports per-artifact diffs. This is the closest thing to a
260: mechanical parity gate and it is the only stage that proves *behaviour* rather
261: than structure.
262: 
263: ### Stage 6 — Map to Aura3D
264: 
265: Map the extracted mechanic to an Aura3D surface **and** to the parity items it
266: needs. If the parity item is not built, the mapping is a plan, not a port.
267: 
268: | Crayon mechanic | Aura3D surface | Status | Parity gate |
269: | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Headless defaults to true.\n- Actions: `goto` (`destination`, `wait_until` = `commit` | `domcontentloaded` |\n  `load`), `click`, `fill`, `press`, `select_option`, `check` / `uncheck`,\n  `wait_for` (`state` = `attached` | `detached` | `visible` | `hidden`),\n  `wait_for_timeout` (`duration_ms`). Every action needs a unique `step_id`.\n- Locators: `test_id` (`value`), `role` (`role` + `name`), `css` (`selector`).\n- Capture sections: `screenshot`, `dom`, `accessibility`, `url`, `history`,\n  `storage`. Locator actions resolve on the shell\npage; keyboard events reach whatever is focused but cannot be aimed at a frame\nelement. Treat the REA scenario as the **shell-level** fixture (load,\nstart, pause, restart) and the raw CDP script as the **in-game** fixture.\n\n**Assert only what is observable.** REA does not evaluate JavaScript, so a\nfixture cannot read `lap`, `heat`, or `pickupCount` from game memory. #### Response

Honest verdict: **high value as a schema and boundary oracle, low value as the analysis engine.** Roughly 8/10 for documentation correctness, 2/10 for actually reverse-engineering the game.

**Where it earned its place**

| Job | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `__describe__` on `capture_browser_scenario` | Gave the exact action, locator, and capture enums. Found that `console` is an event, not a capture section. |
| `__describe__` on `compare_web_captures` | Found the real bug: `before`/`after` need an `inspection`; scenarios go in `before_scenario`/`after_scenario`. Stage 5 was wrong. |
| Error surfaces | Produced the exact `target_unavailable` / `reason: target_not_allowed` / *“must be an HTTP(S) page”* text that is now a failure-mode row. |
| `list_browser_targets` | Showed the iframe is filtered as `non_page` even with no origin filter — which is why raw `/json/list` is required. |
| `capture_web_screenshot` | Worked cleanly on the shell page; rejected the frame as expected. |
| Catalog discovery | `__list__` confirmed there is no “guidance” or “workflow” tool — schemas are the guidance. |

**Where it fell down**

- **It cannot touch the actual target.** Every browser tool rejects the `about:srcdoc` frame. That is the game. The MCP can only see the shell.
- **It cannot evaluate JavaScript.** By design, no `evaluate` action exists, so none of the four runtime probes (node materials, `BatchedMesh`, composer, GLSL) can run through it.
- **Heavy bundles kill it.** `analyze_web_bundle` previously exited with a V8 stack on the 1.37 MB vendor chunk. That chunk is shell code, not game code — so the MCP crashed analyzing the wrong artifact.
- **Its schemas are awkward to consume.** `__describe__` responses are deep enough to blow the Code Mode serializer at depth 32; I had to flatten them in code.
- **No prose guidance.** It tells you the shape of a valid call, not which call answers your question. That mapping is still on the agent.

**Bottom line**

The MCP materially improved the runbook because it is authoritative about its own contract — and that contract exposed two false claims I had written. But it never analyzed the game. The division that actually works is:

- **REA MCP/CLI:** schemas, page-level inspection/scenarios/screenshots, and local static analysis of extracted files.
- **Raw CDP:** frame discovery, module extraction, runtime probes, in-game input.

For this task I’d keep it in the loop for the schema and page-level work, and not expect it to be the reverse-engineering engine.

Fence helper:
```js
function fence(text, lang="text") {
  const runs = text.match(/`+/g) || [];
  const max = runs.reduce((m,r)=>Math.max(m,r.length),0);
  const f = "`".repeat(Math.max(3, max+1));
  return `${f}${lang}\n${text}\n${f}`;
}
```
